Issues.Title: Fix Native AOT completion for JS-invoked Tasks
Issues.Body:
# Fix Native AOT completion for JS-invoked Tasks

Resolve JS-invoked task promises under Native AOT

## Description

Native AOT applications could complete a `[JSInvokable]` method in managed code without resolving or rejecting the promise returned by `invokeMethodAsync`. Non-generic async methods could expose an internal `Task<VoidTaskResult>`, while generic `Task<T>` and `ValueTask<T>` paths depended on dynamically constructed generic helpers that might not have native code available.

This change:

- uses the declared `[JSInvokable]` return type to identify non-generic `Task` and `ValueTask` results
- avoids dynamically constructing `TaskResultGetter<VoidTaskResult>` under Native AOT
- uses preserved `Task<T>.Result` and `ValueTask<T>.AsTask` members when dynamic code is unavailable
- ensures faulted and canceled asynchronous invocations report one failure completion
- adds unit coverage and a Native AOT browser matrix for completed and asynchronous `Task`, `ValueTask`, `Task<T>`, and `ValueTask<T>` methods

Fixes #69432

## Customer Impact

In Native AOT-published Blazor Server applications, JavaScript awaiting a `[JSInvokable]` method that returns `Task`, `ValueTask`, `Task<T>`, or `ValueTask<T>` can wait indefinitely even after the managed method completes. Applications that use the returned promise for backpressure or state transitions can become permanently stuck and cannot recover without reloading. There is no application-level workaround that preserves asynchronous callbacks other than changing the callback to a synchronous method or avoiding Native AOT.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

This is a gap in the existing Native AOT JS interop implementation rather than a regression from a previously supported release.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

The change is localized to completion handling for JS-invoked asynchronous .NET methods. Existing dynamic-code paths remain unchanged; Native AOT uses preserved members on the already-closed `Task<T>` and `ValueTask<T>` types.
## Verification

- [x] Manual (required)
- [x] Automated

Automated verification:

- Native AOT JS interop E2E tests: 2 passed, including all eight completed/asynchronous return shapes and exact application-defined value-type result serialization
- targeted JS interop dispatcher tests: 5 passed

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

No packaging changes.

----

## When servicing release/2.3

- [ ] Make necessary changes in eng/PatchConfig.props

Not applicable to `release/11.0`.

Issues.Title: [pr-attention-queue] Fix merge-state refresh and Pulse detector auth
Issues.Body:
This PR addresses two separate Pulse reliability failures: stale merge-state information in the collector, and a mismatched detector credential after the inline-detection workaround. It includes current `main` through `7cc41c501115f365c0b7f1b50ebaa134a328f0e5`.

## 1. Refresh both merge-state values together

When GitHub initially returns `UNKNOWN`, the existing retry updated `mergeable` but left `mergeStateStatus` stale. An approved PR with passing checks could therefore remain under **Waiting on CI**, disappear from both the **Ready to merge** and **Verify discussion before merge** views, or fail to surface a required branch update.

The retry now requests and stores both values together. A small null-handling guard keeps incomplete mergeability information from granting clearance. **The existing CI, approval, and discussion rules still apply; this changes their inputs, not the rules.** Retry selection, batch sizes, and limits are unchanged.

Three regression cases fail on the original code and pass with this change:

| Refreshed state | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clean, approved, passing checks, clear discussion | Waiting on CI | Ready to merge |
| Same state, with a current unresolved discussion | Waiting on CI | Verify discussion before merge only |
| Branch behind its base | Waiting on CI | Author/maintainer asked to update the branch |

All **14 conservative controls** pass before and after, including unknown/missing data, conflicts, blocked states, failed checks, and requested changes. The focused suite passes **17/17**. Recorded same-head GitHub responses for #68146 and #65785 also reproduce both cold-input omissions through the actual collector, sanitizer, and renderer. The fix restores #68146 to the ready view while keeping #65785 only in discussion verification; cases where GitHub already returned a known state continue to pass unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Merge-state regression details</summary>

The frozen baseline is `main` at `e10a071e2c7744370cb4652bfc40b31c9de7853b`. Transport fixtures return only fields requested by the GraphQL query.

Independent scratch-copy checks confirm that query-only and assignment-only changes are insufficient: both still fail the relevant material assertions. Removing the null guard also fails the deliberately malformed-response control by incorrectly granting merge eligibility; this is not a claim that GitHub returned null in the observed runs.

</details>

## 2. Use the selected PAT-pool credential for inline detection

In [scheduled run 35730232915](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35730232915), the main agent completed collection, but the detector's provider `/models` and `/responses` calls returned **HTTP 401**. Detection produced no verdict and publication was skipped. The missing `THREAT_DETECTION_RESULT` was secondary to that authentication failure.

The inline workaround in #69419 exposed a configuration difference: Pulse explicitly sets the detector's engine/model, so the inline compiler does not inherit the main engine's environment. The generated detector consequently used `secrets.COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, while the main agent used the selected PAT-pool expression. The logs do not establish whether that standalone secret was absent, expired, revoked, or otherwise rejected.

The detector now explicitly binds `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` to **exactly the main agent's existing PAT-pool expression**. This aligns Pulse with the other five workflows changed by #69419, which already compile both stages to the same selected credential. There is no new secret, permission, pool allocation, or sandbox exposure.

The lock was regenerated—not hand-edited—with **gh-aw v0.88.7** and the existing singleton `gpt-5.6-sol` compile policy. Regeneration also restores that required model allowlist on the inline detector. The inline workaround remains enabled, detection failures still block publication, and the runtime pins, schedule, model fallback/steering restrictions, and provider-token exclusion remain intact.

### Generated-output regression evidence

- Credential equality fails against the integrated pre-fix lock for the expected mismatch.
- Recompiling the unchanged source restores the model policy but still fails credential equality: **11/12 controls pass**.
- With the explicit binding, **12/12 controls pass**, including direct `pat_pool` dependency/environment, inline failure gating, singleton model policy, and provider-token exclusion.
- Exact generated-content comparison confirms the only runtime change versus the equivalently recompiled baseline is the detector credential. Other differences are metadata and removal of the standalone-secret dependency.

The existing schedule test now checks the exact setup SHA already pinned by upstream rather than the old tag spelling.

## Validation commands

All commands passed on the final combined changes:

```powershell
pwsh -NoProfile -File .github\workflows\pr-attention-pulse\Compile-PRAttentionPulse.ps1
pwsh -NoProfile -File .github\workflows\pr-attention-pulse\Compile-PRAttentionPulse.ps1 -Validate
pwsh -NoProfile -File .github\workflows\pr-attention-pulse-tests\Test-PulseReviewRequirements.ps1
pwsh -NoProfile -File .github\workflows\pr-attention-pulse-tests\Test-PRAttentionPulse.ps1
pwsh -NoProfile -File .github\skills\pr-attention-queue\tests\Test-PRAttentionQueue.ps1
```

Strict compilation and compiler validation produce byte-identical locks. The complete Pulse suite passes, including **67/67 merge-requirement** and **45/45 comment-coverage** cases; the complete Queue suite also passes. Scoped and staged `git diff --check` pass.

## Hosted validation

A manual dispatch of the exact PR head (`89c3f8cf1b401d8b7fe80174ce81a384c2b2cbc8`) completed successfully in [run 35788119050](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35788119050).

- `pre_activation`, `pat_pool`, `activation`, target validation, `agent`, `detection`, and `safe_outputs` all succeeded.
- The detector made five `gpt-5.6-sol` `/responses` requests, all returning HTTP 200; no provider authentication failure occurred.
- Threat detection emitted a clean verdict and, because detection is fail-closed, publication was allowed to proceed.
- Safe outputs successfully replaced the body of #69328.
- The published issue body exactly matches the trusted `pulse-body.md` artifact: 19,860 characters and SHA-256 `4C2F353DEAB2C17BE52E9A77F8F82656FE162B4CF9E80D8909161930582E18C4`.

This validates the complete hosted path for the PAT selected by that run. It does not independently validate every PAT entry in the pool or establish why the old standalone credential was rejected.

The merge-state reproduction does not establish the cause of the September 17 omissions or claim that the September 21 published report was wrong. Dashboard presentation and publishing code are unchanged.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0] Replace explicit command after navigation with automatic dismissing by ChromeDriver.
Issues.Body:
Backport of #69416 to release/11.0

/cc @ilonatommy

# Replace explicit command after navigation with automatic dismissing by ChromeDriver.

Test change only.

## Description

The affected `NavigationLock` E2E tests correctly register and trigger a `beforeunload` handler, but ChromeDriver handles the prompt before it can be retrieved through Selenium's classic `SwitchTo().Alert()` API. The explicit dismissal consequently fails with `NoAlertPresentException`.

This behavior is tracked by [Chromium issue 428153658](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/428153658).

This change configures dedicated browser sessions used by the affected tests to dismiss `beforeunload` prompts automatically. Dismissing the prompt cancels the attempted navigation and keeps the browser on the current page, preserving the behavior previously requested through the explicit `Alert().Dismiss()` calls.

The prompt behavior is opt-in and does not affect other routing or browser tests.

Fixes #66041  
Fixes #66043

None, it's increasing test coverage.

Issues.Title: Stabilize Virtualize anchor mode test setup
Issues.Body: Recent `AnchorMode_WindowScroll_End_PrependAtTop_ViewportStaysStable` failures occurred before the prepend operation. The test found rendered rows but no row intersecting the viewport, causing `GetItemPositionInViewport` to fail with: ```text Assert.NotNull() Failure: Value is null ``` The previous setup configured the scenario through several live UI transitions. Each transition could initiate rendering, observer callbacks, scroll correction, or an asynchronous `ItemsProvider` request. The item-count checks could then succeed against an intermediate set of rows without proving that the final viewport was ready for measurement. Configuring the component while its list is unloaded avoids creating these intermediate `Virtualize` states. The test now creates one `Virtualize` instance with its final configuration and waits for the resulting viewport to settle before capturing the baseline position.

Issues.Title: Prevent documentation workflow tool retry loops
Issues.Body:
## Summary

- clarify that trusted migration, breaking-change, and release-note directories are placement metadata only when those surfaces are independently required
- prevent creation of a future-version release-note entry point or `includes` hierarchy when the docs repository does not already have that structure
- stop denied-tool retry loops and require `draft_failed` for required operations that cannot be completed with permitted tools
- add `mkdir` as the only new bash command so genuinely required documentation/article directories can be created while the semantic guardrails prevent unnecessary release-note hierarchy creation
- preserve `max-turns: 100` and keep wildcard shell access plus other broad or file-execution commands unavailable
- add focused regression assertions for prompt policy, shell permissions, and the unchanged turn cap

## Root cause

[PR Documentation Check run 35718934996](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35718934996/job/106717623435) successfully completed trusted setup, authentication, source analysis, and the canonical conceptual documentation edit. It then repeatedly tried excluded shell commands while attempting to create a nonexistent ASP.NET Core 12 release-note hierarchy. The agent exhausted the invocation cap with `429 Maximum LLM invocations exceeded (100 / 100)` before emitting `notify_source_pr`, so downstream output validation failed.

This change fixes the control loop in the prompt and adds narrowly scoped defense-in-depth for legitimate directory creation. It adds only `mkdir`; it does not add wildcard bash, network commands, file-execution commands, or a higher turn cap.

## Validation

- `python -m unittest discover -s .github/workflows/pr-docs-check -p "test_*.py"`
- `gh aw compile pr-docs-check --strict --validate --approve`
- inspected the generated lock command to confirm `mkdir` is allowed while `install`, `touch`, `cp`, `python3`, `curl`, `base64`, `rm`, and wildcard agent shell grants remain absent
- `git diff --check`

Issues.Title: Replace explicit command after navigation with automatic dismissing by ChromeDriver.
Issues.Body:
It looks like the affected `NavigationLock` E2E tests started failing after CI upgraded ChromeDriver.

The tests correctly register and trigger a `beforeunload` handler, but newer ChromeDriver versions automatically handle `beforeunload` prompts before they can be accessed through the classic WebDriver alert API. As a result, the following call throws `NoAlertPresentException`:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/e10a071e2c7744370cb4652bfc40b31c9de7853b/src/Components/test/E2ETest/ServerExecutionTests/NavigationLockPrerenderingTest.cs#L40

This is tracked by the [ChromeDriver issue](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/428153658). 

This PR configures routing test sessions to dismiss `beforeunload` prompts automatically.

Such dismissing cancels the attempted navigation and keeps the browser on the current page - the same action previously was performed by the explicit dismiss.

Issues.Body:
Fixes two failures observed in [workflow run 35706277858](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35706277858).

The safe-output preflight validator used a single `elif` chain for drafted outcomes. A valid `docs_pr_action: created` with exactly one `create_pull_request` made the error predicate false, then fell through to the final rejection. This change validates `created` and `updated` in explicit branches and adds positive preflight coverage for both paths while retaining the existing negative cases.

The custom `Notify source PR` job attempted to comment on the merged source PR with `issues: write` but only `pull-requests: read`, which produced `403 Resource not accessible by integration`. The job now grants both `issues: write` and `pull-requests: write` and continues to use the native `${{ github.token }}` for the source-repository comment.

The Copilot PAT pool remains inference-only. Pool PATs have only Copilot Requests (Read), so they are not used for source comments or any repository mutation. Tests enforce that the pool expression is confined to the engine configuration. The existing authentication split is preserved: the native workflow token handles ordinary dotnet/aspnetcore operations, while the docs GitHub App remains limited to AspNetCore.Docs and AspNetCore.Docs.Automation.

Issues.Title: Blazor SSR: exception in OnInitializedAsync during a named-form POST bypasses ErrorBoundary and returns a bare 400 "form not found"
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

### Description

When a named form (`EditForm FormName="..."` or `<form @formname="...">`) is posted to, Blazor SSR resolves *which* form was submitted by rendering the component tree until it finds the matching form marker. If an exception is thrown during that POST render pass (e.g. in `OnInitializedAsync`) *before* the form element is reached:

- `ErrorBoundary.OnErrorAsync` **does** catch the exception and renders the configured fallback UI, as expected.
- However, because rendering never reached the named form marker, the framework's named-form resolution independently concludes "form not found" and the endpoint invoker replaces the **entire HTTP response** with a bare `400 Bad Request`.
- The `ErrorBoundary`'s rendered fallback output is discarded. The end user gets a blank/generic 400 response instead of the app's error UI, and the original exception is not surfaced anywhere in the response (only in server logs).

This defeats the purpose of `ErrorBoundary` for any request that happens to be a POST to a named form, which is surprising and undocumented — nothing in the forms or error-handling docs indicates that error-boundary fallback rendering can be silently overridden this way.

### Expected Behavior

If `ErrorBoundary` catches an exception and renders fallback content, that response should be returned to the client (e.g. `200 OK` with the fallback UI), consistent with normal (non-form) SSR requests. Named-form resolution failing due to an *exception* during rendering should not be treated the same as a genuinely malformed/forged POST.

At minimum, this behavior should be documented, since it's a significant, easy-to-hit gap for any app that wraps forms in `ErrorBoundary` (which the docs otherwise recommend as the standard error-handling pattern).

The reason this is easy to hit, is because any API based initialization logic that can fail is often in OnInitializedAsync. The Form not found error  should maybe wrap the pre-existing exception and be handled via the error boundary after all.

https://github.com/shinkathe/blazor-error-repro/tree/main/repro

Issues.Title: [Native AOT] JSInvokable Task completes in .NET but invokeMethodAsync promise never settles
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I searched the existing issues.

Related: #64137 describes how `TaskGenericsUtil.GetTaskResult` observes `Task<VoidTaskResult>`, but that issue did not identify a user-visible failure.

### Describe the bug

In a Native AOT-published Blazor Server app, a JavaScript call to an instance `[JSInvokable]` method that returns `Task` can execute and complete in managed code while the promise returned by `DotNetObjectReference.invokeMethodAsync` never settles.

This can permanently block JavaScript code that applies backpressure based on that promise:

```js
let inFlight = false;

function update() {
    if (inFlight) {
        return;
    }

    inFlight = true;
    console.debug('Sending update');
    dotNetRef.invokeMethodAsync('SetValueAsync', 42)
        .then(() => console.debug('Update completed'))
        .catch(error => console.error('Update failed', error))
        .finally(() => inFlight = false);
}
```

The component callback has this shape:

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public async Task SetValueAsync(int value)
{
    logger.LogDebug("Received update");
    await InvokeAsync(() =>
    {
        _value = value;
        StateHasChanged();
    });
    logger.LogDebug("Completed update");
}
```

Observed under Native AOT:

- The browser logs `Sending update`.
- The server logs both `Received update` and `Completed update`.
- The browser never logs `Update completed` or `Update failed`.
- The promise remains pending, so `finally` never runs.
- No exception is reported in the browser console or server logs.

Changing the callback to synchronous `void` fixes the problem while continuing to call it with `invokeMethodAsync`:

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public void SetValue(int value)
{
    _value = value;
    StateHasChanged();
}
```

```js
await dotNetRef.invokeMethodAsync('SetValue', 42);
```

The promise then settles normally and repeated calls succeed.

### Expected behavior

When a `[JSInvokable]` method returns a successfully completed `Task`, the promise returned by `invokeMethodAsync` should resolve. If returning `Task` is unsupported under Native AOT, publishing should produce an actionable warning and the browser promise should reject instead of remaining pending forever.

### Suspected cause

`DotNetDispatcher.EndInvokeDotNetAfterTask` obtains the result using:

```csharp
TaskGenericsUtil.GetTaskResult(task)
```

`TaskGenericsUtil.GetTaskResult` examines `task.GetType()` and dynamically creates a closed helper:

```csharp
Activator.CreateInstance(
    typeof(TaskResultGetter<>).MakeGenericType(taskResultType))
```

A non-generic `Task` returned from an async method or framework helper can have a concrete runtime type based on `Task<VoidTaskResult>`. Under Native AOT, the dynamically constructed `TaskResultGetter<VoidTaskResult>` is not available. The exception appears to fault the `ContinueWith` callback used by `EndInvokeDotNetAfterTask` before `JSRuntime.EndInvokeDotNet` sends either a success or failure completion to JavaScript.

This path currently has trimming suppression with the justification that JS-invokable return types are retained, but the dynamically constructed helper itself also needs to be AOT-safe.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a Blazor Web App using Interactive Server rendering.
2. Register a component instance with JavaScript using `DotNetObjectReference.Create(this)`.
3. Add a `[JSInvokable]` method returning `Task`, as shown above.
4. Call it from JavaScript with `invokeMethodAsync` and attach `then`, `catch`, and `finally` handlers.
5. Publish self-contained with Native AOT:

```console
dotnet publish -c Debug -r win-x64 --self-contained true -p:PublishAot=true
```

6. Run the published app and trigger the callback.

The managed method completes, but none of the JavaScript promise handlers execute. Change the method to synchronous `void`, republish, and the promise settles.

### Additional context

Reproduced on Windows x64 with:

```text
.NET SDK: 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128
Microsoft.AspNetCore.App: 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128
Microsoft.NETCore.App: 11.0.0-rc.1.26425.128
OS: Windows 10.0.26200, win-x64
```

The original application registered source-generated JSON resolvers with `AddInteractiveServerComponents`. Adding source-generated metadata for `object` did not change the behavior. Callback arguments were primitive integers and were deserialized successfully, as shown by the managed entry log.

Issues.Title: Fix MVC1004 false positive for [FromServices] parameters
Issues.Body:

- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making.

Fix MVC1004 false positive for `[FromServices]` parameters.

## Description

`TopLevelParameterNameAnalyzer` (MVC1004) warns when a controller action
parameter has the same name (case-insensitive) as a public property of its
own complex type, because that can make model binding ambiguous. However, a
parameter injected from services with `[FromServices]` is **not** model
bound, so a name collision with a property of the service type cannot cause a
binding ambiguity — the warning is a false positive.

This changes `IsProblematicParameter` to skip parameters annotated with
`[FromServices]`, mirroring the existing `[FromBody]` exclusion. The
`FromServicesAttribute` type is resolved through the analyzer's existing
`SymbolCache` in the same way as the other well-known MVC attributes.

This is a **non-breaking** change: it only removes an incorrect diagnostic;
no MVC1004 report that is currently correct is affected.

Reproduction (from the issue):

```csharp
public class HomeController : Controller
{
    [HttpGet]
    public async Task<ActionResult> Get([FromServices] SiteSettingsService settings) { /* ... */ }
    //                                                                    ^^^^^^^^ MVC1004 (before this fix)
}

public class SiteSettingsService(AppDbContext db)
{
    public SiteSettings Settings => /* ... */;   // property name collides with the parameter name
}
```

## Test verification (RED → GREEN)

Added `NoDiagnosticsAreReturnedForFromServicesParameters` to
`TopLevelParameterNameAnalyzerTest`. It fails on the unmodified analyzer and
passes with the fix.

RED — new test on the target branch with the fix reverted (only the analyzer
source stashed):

```
// /0/Test0.cs(7,106): warning MVC1004: Property on type 'NoDiagnosticsAreReturnedForFromServicesParametersService' has the same name as parameter 'settings'. This may result in incorrect model binding. ...
Failed!  - Failed:     1, Passed:     0, Skipped:     0, Total:     1 - Mvc.Analyzers.Test.dll (net11.0)
```

GREEN — same test with the fix applied:

```
Passed!  - Failed:     0, Passed:     1, Skipped:     0, Total:     1 - Mvc.Analyzers.Test.dll (net11.0)
```

No regressions in the full analyzer test class:

```
Passed!  - Failed:     0, Passed:    27, Skipped:     0, Total:    27 - Mvc.Analyzers.Test.dll (net11.0)
```

Command: `./.dotnet/dotnet test src/Mvc/Mvc.Analyzers/test/Mvc.Analyzers.Test.csproj --filter "FullyQualifiedName~TopLevelParameterNameAnalyzer" -c Debug`

Fixes #63888

Issues.Title: Use committed local criteria and concise output for PR reviews
Issues.Body:
# Use committed local criteria and concise output for PR reviews

## Description

Address two reported usability problems: a servicing PR can target a branch that lacks the reviewer guides (as encountered with #69401), and ordinary interactive results should not dump the full review state.

1. **Use committed local guidance.** Freeze the current repository's `HEAD` once as `LOCAL_SHA`, at invocation start before GitHub retrieval. Read guides, delegated policies, and optional API design criteria from that commit. Guidance edits must be committed but need not be pushed; uncommitted edits are ignored. Missing required committed inputs produce an explicit block, not a fallback or successful no-findings result.
2. **Return concise results by default.** Show actionable findings and material limitations. Retain detailed structured diagnostics when explicitly requested.
3. **Adapt the hosted `/review` caller.** Prepare the immutable default-branch event revision with an explicit checkout step while keeping gh-aw's automatic PR-head checkout disabled. Allow the required Git reads and pass the frozen local criteria identity to workers. Use `git show` from the verified repository root; this equivalent read form works with the pinned CLI's scoped permission grant. Replace the obsolete target-base/bundle instructions. Preserve source-only review, topic accounting, deduplication, and the existing frozen-SHA COMMENT-only output adapter.
4. **Double the main reviewer turn limit from 200 to 400.** Run [35755119618](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35755119618) failed with `Maximum LLM invocations exceeded (206 / 200)`. The separate detection limit remains 20; other budgets are unchanged.

The GitHub PR still defines the reviewed code. Product source uses `HEAD_SHA`; authoritative target documents use `BASE_SHA`. Local criteria do not themselves establish that older target code violates a binding contract. Topic coverage, one independent worker per topic, dispatch/retry/fallback accounting, and candidate-validation gates remain intact. The reviewer agent does not prepare or modify the workspace; the hosted caller prepares it before invocation. Local-diff review and execution of PR builds/tests are not added. No product changes are included.

## Validation

- The focused five-case native suite passed all 44 graders: main/API criteria, historical release criteria, missing committed guidance despite a working-tree copy, concise findings, and incomplete results. Native evaluation executor/judge were pinned to `gpt-5.6-sol`.
- All 37 deterministic guidance-source tests pass, including portable fixture preparation, actual Vally workspace-preservation checks, literal-SHA/path read assertions, and contradictory blocked-output controls. The relevant negative controls rejected the earlier implementation before correction.
- All six hosted-caller policy tests pass; five compatibility/turn-limit checks reject the previous caller, while the unchanged source-only/publication boundaries remain green. Run with `python3 .github/workflows/pull-request-review/test_workflow_policy.py`.
- Strict compilation with the deployed gh-aw v0.88.7 succeeded. Generated configuration has exactly one reviewer-revision checkout in the agent job, no automatic PR-head checkout, scoped Git-read grants, and a 400-turn main reviewer limit. The source and generated lock file are both included.
- A bounded actual Copilot CLI 1.0.80 smoke using `gpt-5.6-sol` successfully resolved root/HEAD once and read both guides and optional API criteria at that literal SHA with the final command grants. Earlier `git -C` grant probes were denied; the final `git show` form succeeded. This was a command-access smoke, not native skill or full-panel validation.
- Earlier live native preflight and full source-only review of the now-merged #69401 completed. The full review recovered an initial briefing handoff failure with bounded retries; it does not establish hosted compatibility or review-quality equivalence.

**Validation boundary:** the updated hosted action has not been dispatched. Compilation, generated configuration, local regression tests, and the pinned CLI command-access smoke do not prove end-to-end hosted execution or positive-finding publication. No claim is made that 400 turns guarantees completion. The local-freeze source-order check does not simulate a real review interrupted by a concurrent edit. No PR product code, builds, or tests were executed.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0] Avoid false positive prepend detection that causes backward scroll jumps
Issues.Body:
Wait for https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69362 merge before touching this one.

Backport the Virtualize anchoring and async-provider fixes from #69362.

## Description

This change fixes multiple related `Virtualize` issues when an asynchronous items provider changes while the user is scrolling:

- Compare items at the same global index across provider windows, preventing ordinary scrolling and appends from being misclassified as prepends.
- Preserve overlapping-window identity when scrolling moves past the previously rendered first item.
- Prevent canceled refreshes from overwriting a newer committed provider window.
- Reuse bounded prefetched rows for small prepends and End-tail appends while limiting prepend look-ahead to explicit data refreshes.
- Track Start/top follow intent independently from End/bottom follow intent.
- Restore table anchors during the matching DOM mutation so Server rendering does not expose a shifted frame.
- Preserve anchor snapshots for layouts using native browser scroll anchoring.
- Prevent Start-mode appends from racing an after-spacer callback and incorrectly pinning the viewport to the new tail.
- Materialize custom-provider results once so lazy or single-pass sequences are not enumerated repeatedly.

Fixes #69380  
Fixes #69381

## Customer Impact

Applications using virtualized live data, including Aspire Dashboard and virtualized QuickGrid scenarios, can experience:

- reverse-direction scroll jumps while new data arrives;
- visible content moving or disappearing during prepends;
- Start mode unexpectedly following appended tail items;
- duplicate provider requests for the same update;
- skipped or delayed materialization during continuous updates;
- stale provider windows being displayed after cancellation;
- failures with lazy or single-pass provider results.

The issues affect both Server and WebAssembly rendering and are most visible with delayed providers, continuously updating data, table virtualization, and fresh item instances returned from each provider call.

There is no complete application-level workaround. Applications can reduce some symptoms by avoiding continuous updates or virtualization, but cannot reliably prevent the provider-window and anchoring races.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [X] No

Net10 didn't have viewport stabilization at all so it is not a regression in comparison to the previous version.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [x] Medium
- [ ] Low

The changes affect internal Virtualize provider-window, anchoring, cancellation, and JavaScript observer behavior. There are no new public APIs or packaging changes. Risk is mitigated by targeted unit, browser, Server, WebAssembly, QuickGrid, table, fixed-height, and variable-height coverage.

- [x] Automated

Issues.Title: Remove inline threat detection workaround after gh-aw update
Issues.Body:
## Summary

Remove the temporary inline threat-detection workaround introduced by #69419 once a gh-aw release containing github/gh-aw#61857 is available.

## Background

All six agentic workflows temporarily set:

```yaml
features:
  gh-aw-detection: false
```

This keeps threat detection enabled but selects the legacy inline implementation to avoid the `threat-detect` v0.5.1 result-sink failure. The defect was confirmed in these `test-quarantine` runs:

- https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35436751188
- https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/actions/runs/35587722124

- `browsertesting-deps-update`
- `community-pr-issue-check`
- `cswin32-update`
- `issue-triage-agent`
- `pr-attention-pulse`
- `test-quarantine`

`test-quarantine` and `pr-attention-pulse` are configured fail closed, so detector tooling failures block their safe outputs. The other four workflows continue on detection errors, so the external-detector defect can otherwise be masked by an overall successful workflow result.

## Completion criteria

- update the local gh-aw compiler to a release containing github/gh-aw#61857
- remove `features.gh-aw-detection: false` from all six workflow Markdown sources listed above
- regenerate all six corresponding lockfiles with the updated compiler
- verify the generated workflows use the fixed external `threat-detect` version

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

The is a problem nesting embedded resources.  I was experimenting with nesting .cshtml files using the existing rules and did this:

Modal.cs (bootstrap modal web component)
   -> Modal.cs.cshtml (it's view file)

`Modal.cs.cshtml` is set to Embedded Resource, and clearly shows it, but is completed IGNORED by the build process (simply open the DLL in a text editor [such as Notepad++] and scroll to the bottom and look for text).  If I rename the file to "Modal.cshtml" instead it works perfectly fine!  :/  I don't think whether or not a file is embedded should have and role in excluding a file from being embedded so this seems like a bug to me.

Yes, I'm aware of upcoming nesting controls in v15.6, but I'm not able to install it yet, and regardless, this should work fine, so it should be looked into nonetheless.

Just to add: I'm using wild-cards to include the file.  If I explicitly add it I get this:

`Duplicate 'EmbeddedResource' items were included. ...`

So it's clearly found.  It's obviously something up with the build process not finding the nested file.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Title: Add automation to create docs tracking issues for breaking changes
Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
```

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and MVC API analyzers are deprecated
Issues.Body:
## Description

The `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` MSBuild property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. When `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will now emit warning `ASPDEPR007`.

## Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

## Previous behavior

Previously, developers could set `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` in their Web SDK projects to enable MVC API analyzers without any warnings or deprecation notices.

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

The project would build successfully without any deprecation warnings.

## New behavior

Starting in .NET 10 Preview 7, when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will emit warning `ASPDEPR007`:

```
warning ASPDEPR007: The IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
```

The analyzers will continue to function, but developers will receive this deprecation warning during compilation.

## Type of breaking change

- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

## Reason for change

## Reason for change

The MVC API analyzers were originally introduced to help keep return types and attributes in sync for API controllers, ensuring consistency between method signatures and their corresponding OpenAPI documentation. These analyzers provided compile-time validation to catch mismatches between declared return types and the actual types returned by controller actions.

However, with the introduction of Minimal APIs and the `TypedResults` pattern, the .NET ecosystem has evolved toward a more type-safe approach for API development. `TypedResults` provides compile-time guarantees about response types without requiring additional analyzers, making the MVC API analyzers redundant for modern .NET applications. In .NET 10, `TypedResults` are supported in controller-based APIs.

**Previous approach with MVC API analyzers:**
```csharp
[HttpGet]
[ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)]
[ProducesResponseType(404)]
public async Task<ActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    if (product == null)
        return NotFound(); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType(404)
    
    return Ok(product); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)
}
```

**Or with controller actions using TypedResults:**
```csharp
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    return product == null 
        ? TypedResults.NotFound() 
        : TypedResults.Ok(product);
}
```

The `TypedResults` pattern eliminates the need for separate analyzers because the return type itself (`Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>`) explicitly declares all possible response types at compile time. This approach is more maintainable, provides better IntelliSense support, and automatically generates accurate OpenAPI documentation without additional tooling.

As the .NET ecosystem continues to embrace `TypedResults` as the recommended pattern for API development, the MVC API analyzers have become obsolete and are being deprecated to streamline the development experience.

## Recommended action

Developers should:

1. **Remove the deprecated property**: Remove `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` from your project files to eliminate the warning.

2. **Suppress the warning temporarily**: If you need to continue using the deprecated analyzers temporarily, you can suppress the warning:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ASPDEPR007</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

3. **Migrate to TypedResults**: Migrate to the `TypedResults` pattern documented above to ensure better consistency between application behavior and OpenAPI documentation.

## Affected APIs

- MSBuild property: `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers`
- Associated MVC API analyzers included when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is `true`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Forwarded Headers Middleware Now Ignores X-Forwarded-* Headers from Unknown Proxies
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, the Forwarded Headers Middleware will ignore all `X-Forwarded-*` headers from proxies that are not explicitly configured as trusted.

### Version

.NET 8

### Previous behavior

Previously, the middleware, when not configured to use `X-Forwarded-For`, would process `X-Forwarded-Prefix`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers from any source, potentially allowing malicious or misconfigured proxies/clients to spoof these headers and affect your application's understanding of client information.

### New behavior

With this change, only headers sent by known, trusted proxies (as configured via `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies` and `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownNetworks`) will be processed. Headers from unknown sources will be ignored.

**This is a breaking change**: If your deployment relied on forwarded headers from proxies not configured in your application's trusted proxy list, those headers will no longer be honored.

This can cause behavior like infinite redirects if you're using the Https redirection middleware and using TLS termination in your proxy. Or authentication to fail if using TLS termination and expecting an https request.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The change was made for security hardening, as the proxy and IP lists weren't being applied in all cases.

### Recommended action

- **Review your deployment topology:**  
  Ensure that all legitimate proxy servers in front of your app are properly added to `KnownProxies` or `KnownNetworks` in your `ForwardedHeadersOptions` configuration.
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownProxies = { IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_PROXY_IP") }
  });
  ```
  Or, for a network:
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownNetworks = { new IPNetwork(IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_NETWORK_IP"), PREFIX_LENGTH) }
  });
  ```

- **If you wish to enable previous behavior:**  
  You may need to relax your configuration, but this is **not recommended** due to security risks. You can do this by clearing the `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` lists in `ForwardedHeadersOptions` to allow any proxy or network to forward these headers.

You can also set the `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` environment variable to true, which clears the lists and enables `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto`.

For applications targeting .NET 9.0 or less, you can set the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides.IgnoreUnknownProxiesWithoutFor` [AppContext](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/runtime-libraries/system-appcontext) switch to `"true"` or `1` to get back to the previous behavior. Alternatively, set the `MICROSOFT_ASPNETCORE_HTTPOVERRIDES_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_PROXIES_WITHOUT_FOR` environment variable.

> [!Note]
> In cloud environments, the proxy IP(s) can change over the lifetime of the app and `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` is sometimes used to make forwarded headers work.

### References

- [Forwarded Headers Middleware documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/proxy-load-balancer)

### Affected APIs

`UseForwardedHeaders();`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: dev cert export no longer creates folder
Issues.Body:
### Description

When you export the ASP.NET Core development certificate (used to enable https in local development), it will no longer create the directory into which the certificate is being exported, if that directory doesn’t already exist.

This change first appears in 8.0.10 and 9.0 RC1.

### Version

.NET 8 GA

### Previous behavior

```
dotnet dev-certs https -ep C:\NonExistent\cert.pfx
```

If `C:\NonExistent\` did not exist when the command was run, it would be created (with permissions inherited from the containing directory).

### New behavior

The target directory must exist or the export will fail with a message like `There was an error exporting the HTTPS developer certificate to a file.`

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The development certificate is exported with its private key, so unauthorized access can be very problematic.  It may, nevertheless, be necessary to make it readable to multiple accounts - e.g. if the consuming process will not be run as the current user.  Rather than attempting to determine (and securely establish) permissions for the target directory, `dotnet dev-certs` require that it already exist.

### Recommended action

Create the target directory (with appropriate permissions) before invoking `dotnet dev-certs`.

### Affected APIs

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Handling of middleware types with multiple constructors
Issues.Body:
### Description

Formerly, when a middleware type with multiple satisfiable constructors was instantiated from the dependency injection container, the one with the most parameters would be used.  Now that only happens if the dependency injection container implements [`IServiceProviderIsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.iserviceproviderisservice).

### Version

.NET 9 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Formerly, the first constructor was preferred (when both were satisfied) because it has more parameters.

```csharp
public class CookiePolicyMiddleware
{
    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options, ILoggerFactory factory)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }

    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }
}
```

### New behavior

Now, neither constructor is preferred and construction fails with an error like 
```
System.InvalidOperationException: 'Multiple constructors accepting all given argument types have been found in type 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware'. There should only be one applicable constructor.'
```

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The activation mechanism was [changed](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/55722) to help support keyed dependency injection.

### Recommended action

If this happens and you can't upgrade to a dependency injection container that implements `IServiceProviderIsService`, you can add `ActivatorUtilitiesConstructorAttribute` to the preferred constructor of the affected middleware type.

### Affected APIs

This is [known](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/57231) to cause errors when instantiating `Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware` with [Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection) 7.x.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey has a slightly altered meaning
Issues.Body:
### Description

`DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey` no longer reflects whether the default key is close to its expiration time.

### Version

.NET 9 Preview 3

### Previous behavior

It was an undocumented, but consistent, feature of the API that `ShouldGenerateNewKey` would be true if the default key was within two days (an over-simplification) of its expiration time.  The amount of lead time was based on the polling interval of `ICacheableKeyRingProvider`, which was not something `IDefaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy` should have depended upon (since, for example, alternative implementations would probably not be aware of these details).

### New behavior

If `ShouldGenerateNewKey` is true, it now indicates that either there is no default key or that for some other policy reason (i.e. in a specialized implementation of `IDefaultKeyResolver`, a new key should be generated.  The `ICacheableKeyRingProvider` will make its own decision about whether the expiration time is close enough to warrant generating a new key.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

First, we wanted to change the logic around key generation near expiration time and, second, this makes it more straightforward to implement a custom `IDefaultKeyResolver`.

Note that the documentation for this type already states that "This API supports infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases."

### Recommended action

If you have an `IDefaultKeyResolver` implementation that tries to replicate the expiry logic, that logic can be removed (however, leaving it is fine as well).

If you were consuming `IDefaultKeyResolver` directly, for the express purpose of determining whether expiration was pending and that continues to be important, you can the default key's `ExpirationDate` property directly.

### Affected APIs

Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal.DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Minimal APIs consuming IFormFile or IFormFileCollection parameters require anti-forgery checks
Issues.Body:
### Description

Minimal API endpoints that consume an `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` will now be opted-in to requiring anti-forgery token validation using the new anti-forgery middleware.

### Version

.NET 8 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did not require anti-forgery validation.

### New behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did require anti-forgery validation. An exception will be thrown if the anti-forgery middleware is not registered for an API that defines these input types.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Anti-forgery token validation is a recommended security precaution for APIs that consume data from a form.

### Recommended action

Users can opt out of anti-forgery validation for specific endpoints by using the `DisableAntiforgery` method like so:

```csharp
var app = WebApplication.Create();

app.MapPost("/", (IFormFile formFile) => ...)
  .DisableAntiforgery();

app.Run();
```

### Affected APIs

None.
